inputs.title: The Box That Felt Small
inputs.logline: After Jenny hides the shame of misreading a word, Patch leads the Box Monsters into a shoebox classroom where a giant mistake must become something she can try again with, not something that makes her small.

orderedEvents.text: Jenny stands at the front of the classroom holding her worksheet.
The word BRIDGE is written on the board.
Jenny looks at the word. Her fingers tighten around the paper.
One child lets out a tiny laugh. Another child laughs because the first one did.
Jenny looks at the word again. It feels much bigger now.
Final Frame: Jenny frozen, embarrassed, holding the worksheet close.

beats.storyBeat: Jenny stands in the exposed classroom space and tries to read the line. The ordinary word on the board becomes dangerous through silence, hesitation and the accidental wrong word. The tiny laugh is not cruelly staged, but it is enough to make Jenny’s body close around the worksheet and make her corrected answer come out small.
beats.want: Jenny wants to read the sentence correctly and get safely through her turn.
beats.need: She needs to know that a visible mistake does not reduce her worth.
beats.kidRead: It feels awful when you say something wrong and everyone hears it.
beats.adultRead: A small public stumble can become disproportionately huge inside a sensitive child, even when the adults respond gently.
beats.emotionalIntent: Let the audience feel the blush before the magic begins: embarrassment as a physical freeze, not a lesson.

orderedEvents.text: Shot 03: The Feeling Goes Into The Box
Jenny kneels on her bedroom floor.
Her decorated shoebox sits beside her bed. It has stars, hearts and one wonky rainbow drawn on the lid.
Inside are small treasures: a ribbon, a pebble, an old badge, a folded card.
She places the folded worksheet inside the box.
For a moment, she keeps her hand on it.

beats.storyBeat: In her bedroom, Jenny brings the folded worksheet to her decorated shoebox, a safe place for treasured things. She tries to make the feeling disappear by placing it inside and closing the lid, not noticing that the box has received more than paper: it has received the feeling she cannot carry alone.
beats.want: Jenny wants to put the worksheet away and stop thinking about the classroom mistake.
beats.need: She needs the hidden feeling to be met, not buried.
beats.kidRead: Jenny hides the paper because looking at it hurts.
beats.adultRead: The shoebox becomes a child’s private emotional container: a tender coping strategy that also signals isolation.
beats.emotionalIntent: Make the action intimate and gentle, with the box feeling like a confidant even before the magic answers.

direction.premise: A classroom reading mistake follows Jenny home until her shoebox calls the Box Monsters into a handmade shame world built around one too-large wrong word.
direction.dramaticQuestion: Can the monsters help Jenny carry the mistake differently before shame makes her feel too small to try again?
direction.theme: Getting something wrong does not make you small.
direction.externalJourney: Jenny misreads a word, hides the worksheet in her shoebox, and the monsters travel from The Fold into a cardboard classroom where the mistaken word has swollen into the room’s bossy centrepiece. Their attempted fix fails, then they transform the machine and the meaning of the mistake so Jenny can face the word again.
direction.internalJourney: Jenny moves from public embarrassment, to hiding, to a tiny private openness, to reclaiming the mistake with humour, and finally to trying again while still feeling nervous.
direction.relationshipChanges: Patch begins as a brave responder who wants to help quickly, but earns Jenny’s echo’s trust by sitting with her instead of fixing her. Tilly shifts from controlling the outcome to redesigning her solution around emotional truth. Rumble protects space rather than forcing confidence. Nib’s odd humour becomes the safe bridge between shame and self-acceptance.
direction.emotionalCurve: Quiet pressure builds into embarrassment, then withdrawal, then magical concern. The middle tightens as the wrong fix makes shame heavier. Relief arrives first through being met gently, then through laughter that belongs to Jenny rather than at Jenny. The ending lands in soft courage and secret warmth.
direction.comedyCurve: The comedy starts as character imbalance in The Fold, turns into dry diagnosis and wonky tools, dips during the failed fix, then returns as Nib’s sideways cafe idea makes the mistake feel usable rather than poisonous. The final joke is small, affectionate and earned.
direction.setupPayoffMap: The word BRIDGE becomes BRIGGLE in class, then grows into the shame world’s looming word, then shrinks through laughter, becomes BRIDGE again, and returns in the classroom as a word Jenny can say. Jenny folds the worksheet smaller when ashamed, then later carries it without folding it. The Correct Answer Machine fails, then becomes the Try Again Machine. The shoebox’s first sigh and call pay off as its warm twitch and The Fold lamp glow.

northStar.surfaceStory: Jenny puts the folded worksheet into her decorated shoebox, shuts the lid, and later the box quietly opens to call for help.
northStar.universalTruth: When a child feels ashamed, a safe hiding place can feel like the only way to stop being seen — but hiding the thing also shows exactly where help needs to enter.
northStar.childClearWant: Jenny wants the worksheet gone from sight so the horrible classroom moment will stop replaying in her head.
northStar.emotionalNeed: She needs the feeling to be held safely before it can be faced; this scene must not solve the shame yet, only show that it is too heavy to carry alone.
northStar.falseBeliefUnderPressure: If I shut the mistake away, it will stop meaning something about me.
northStar.relationshipEngine: Jenny treats the shoebox like a trusted keeper of special things; because she trusts it enough to hide the worksheet there, the box receives the feeling and becomes the bridge to The Fold.
northStar.ordinaryLifeTruth: A child often says something 'wasn’t even that funny' when it mattered terribly, then hides the evidence somewhere private because being looked at felt worse than the mistake itself.
northStar.sceneTurn: The shoebox changes from Jenny’s private hiding place into an active caller for help: what she tries to bury becomes the signal.
audienceJourney: Recognise Jenny trying to act like it did not hurt.
Feel the smallness of her folding and closing the worksheet away.
Sense the room go quiet around the hidden feeling.
Feel a warm lift of secret possibility when the shoebox opens and calls.
northStar.finalAfterFeeling: Not fixed; gently alerted. The audience should feel that Jenny is asleep, but the feeling has been heard.
northStar.dialogueSubtractionOpportunity: Do not add any explanation of shame, embarrassment, or magic. Jenny’s handling of the paper, the careful placing in the shoebox, the lid closing, the tremble of the worksheet, and the warm golden opening can carry: 'I feel small,' 'I want it gone,' and 'help is coming.' The locked lines remain verbatim.
northStar.environmentPressure: The bedroom should feel usually safe but now too quiet, with the shoebox, bed, shadows, and still air pressing Jenny toward secrecy. Later the darkness makes the small golden signal feel like a request pushing outward rather than decoration.

treatments.name: The Shoebox Keeps the Secret
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience feels as if they have been allowed into a private, after-school moment Jenny would not want anyone to see. The scene stays gentle and quiet: funny only in Jenny’s tiny attempt to brush off something that clearly hurt. The lift at the end is not a rescue yet, but the warm surprise that the trusted box has understood her better than she understands herself.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: Jenny’s point of view leads the first half: the bedroom is safe, but the worksheet makes it feel unsafe to be seen. Once she sleeps, the emotional point of view transfers to the shoebox, as if the room has been waiting for the hidden feeling to speak.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The dramatic mechanism is a child-sized ritual of denial. Jenny says, “It wasn’t even that funny,” while every small action proves it mattered: careful folding, controlled breathing, choosing the shoebox, pressing the lid shut. The comic surface is the unconvincing little performance of not caring; the emotional truth is that she is giving the shame somewhere to go.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Jenny should not play the feeling as a big cry. She tries to be brisk and practical, almost tidying the problem away. Her hands do the honest acting: holding the worksheet too carefully, folding it smaller than necessary, pausing before the lid closes. “I don’t want to think about it.” lands as a quiet instruction to herself, not an announcement to the room.
treatments.visualGrammar: Wide, low, and handmade-intimate. The shoebox is treated like a small piece of furniture with importance, not a prop insert. Jenny, the bed, the shoebox, and the worksheet share the frame whenever possible so the audience feels the relationship between girl, hiding place, and hidden feeling. Evening bedroom warmth is present but dulled, with the later golden seam kept narrow and sincere.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera behaves like a respectful younger sibling sitting on the floor: close enough to understand, never nosy enough to corner her. It does not rush to her face for proof. It watches her choices in the room and lets the shoebox gradually become the thing with gravity.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Jenny moves with small purposeful tasks at first: enter, kneel, fold, place, close. After the lid shuts, the scene allows stillness to take over. Later, with Jenny asleep, the only movement is the lid easing open and the worksheet trembling, making the tiny motion feel enormous.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Use bedroom depth as layers of safety: bed in the softened background, floor space in the middle, shoebox in the foreground or near foreground without becoming cropped. Treasured things inside the shoebox may be visible only enough to show this is a trusted place, not a bin. Shadows gather around corners after the lid closes, making the golden seam feel like the one place the room can breathe.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: Begin with Jenny trying to move quickly, then let each action slow her down. The fold takes longer than she wants. The placement is too careful to be casual. The lid close is final. Then a time-slip hush: sleeping Jenny, held silence, faint tremble, golden line. Escalation is from concealment to signal, not from quiet to spectacle.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cuts should be rare and motivated by emotional transfer: Jenny carrying the worksheet, Jenny committing it to the box, the room after she sleeps, the box answering. Avoid automatic reaction cutting. Let the audience read the contradiction between her words and behaviour inside wide frames.
treatments.openingImage: Jenny at bedroom-floor height with the folded worksheet in her hands and the decorated shoebox waiting nearby, both small in a room that suddenly feels too quiet.
treatments.closingImage: The shoebox lid open only a narrow crack, a restrained golden seam lighting the folded worksheet while Jenny sleeps in the soft dark beyond.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Do not make this a standard child-at-bedside coverage scene. The danger is over-explaining with face close-ups or making the magic too pretty. Hold the wide frame long enough for the paper, lid, and floor space to carry the shame; make the golden call feel like a small urgent leak of feeling, not a decorative glow effect.

treatments.name: The Worksheet Gets Smaller, Then Louder
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience tracks the worksheet as the embarrassing classroom moment is physically reduced, tucked away, and then impossibly becomes the loudest thing in the room. The scene feels almost like a secret object story: a bit of paper that Jenny wants to silence becomes the messenger that summons help.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The emotional point of view sits on the hidden feeling rather than only on Jenny. Jenny is trying to make the worksheet disappear, but the scene treats the paper as carrying the heat of the memory. Once it enters the shoebox, the box and paper together become the emotional centre.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The mechanism is reversal of scale. Jenny folds the worksheet smaller and smaller to make the mistake matter less, but each fold gives it more dramatic weight. Her line “It wasn’t even that funny.” is played against the absurd precision of someone handling a paper like it might squeak. The later tremble pays off the idea that the feeling was never gone; it was compressed.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Jenny should behave like someone trying not to wake a thought. She handles the worksheet delicately, then too firmly, then delicately again. She may almost over-organise where it goes among the treasured things, as if the right placement can make it harmless. “I don’t want to think about it.” is spoken to the worksheet as much as to herself.
treatments.visualGrammar: Wide frames with the worksheet always legible as an active object in the composition. The room is arranged so the paper’s journey has a clear path: from Jenny’s hands, through open floor space, into the decorated shoebox, then into darkness, then into the golden call. Use negative space around the paper after each fold so its smallness is visible rather than hidden by framing.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera discovers the scene by following the burden, not by waiting for Jenny to arrive at marks. It can drift with the worksheet’s path at a child-room height, keeping Jenny’s full body and the shoebox in view. After she sleeps, the camera no longer follows Jenny; it stays with the paper’s new life inside the box.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: The first half has measured object movement: paper edges bend, hands adjust, lid lowers. Jenny’s body remains contained, but the paper is busy. The second half reverses that: Jenny is still, the room is still, and the worksheet makes the first tiny tremble that proves the hidden feeling is active.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Depth should make the shoebox feel like a destination. The bed and sleeping area sit deeper in frame; the floor path and shoebox occupy the emotional foreground or middle ground. The interior of the box should feel shallow but meaningful, a little cardboard pocket where special things and the unwanted worksheet now share space.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: Rhythm builds through compression: fold, pause; fold, pause; place, longer pause; lid, silence. The later call should not come immediately. Let the audience sit with the closed lid long enough to wonder if that is the end. Then the tremble begins before the glow, so the feeling speaks before the magic answers.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Cut around changes in the worksheet’s status, not around dialogue. One frame may hold Jenny’s line and the folding action together. Another may hold the box closing and the room accepting the silence. The final cut, if used, should feel like time passing from Jenny’s control to the box’s response.

treatments.closingImage: The folded worksheet trembling inside the barely open shoebox, lit by a thin golden line that makes the once-hidden paper impossible to ignore.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: Resist the safe instinct to centre Jenny’s face as the emotional evidence. This version demands that the paper’s path be readable in wide composition. The challenge is to give a flat, folded worksheet enough presence through spacing, light, and timing without resorting to insert-shot thinking or oversized magic.

treatments.name: The Room Holds Its Breath
treatments.audienceExperience: The audience feels the bedroom become too hushed around Jenny, as if every soft object is politely pretending not to notice. The scene begins with ordinary privacy and turns into a quiet call in the dark. The final feeling is a held breath releasing: help is not here yet, but the room has stopped pretending nothing happened.
treatments.emotionalPointOfView: The point of view belongs to the bedroom atmosphere: the familiar room registers Jenny’s attempt to hide the feeling. Jenny is not watched judgmentally; she is held by the space. When she sleeps, the room’s stillness becomes the bridge between her private shame and the secret world that can answer it.
treatments.comicOrDramaticMechanism: The comic surface comes from Jenny’s tiny, unconvincing normalness against a room that seems far too quiet for normal. “It wasn’t even that funny.” hangs in the hush and does not quite land. The dramatic mechanism is environmental pressure: closing the shoebox does not end the moment; it makes the whole room listen harder.
treatments.characterPerformanceStrategy: Jenny should try to move as though this is just putting something away. No grand collapse. She may give the room a small shrug that convinces nobody, then immediately treat the worksheet with more seriousness than her words allow. The second line, “I don’t want to think about it.” is smaller and more honest, with less performance in it.
treatments.visualGrammar: Wide, slightly off-balanced compositions where the bedroom has more quiet space than Jenny wants. Keep full body performance visible, with the shoebox positioned as the one warm, trusted point in the room. Light begins as ordinary evening softness, then drains into a muted bedtime hush before the golden seam gently cuts across the dark.
treatments.cameraCharacterRelationship: The camera is not a companion on the floor or an object follower; it is the room noticing. It may begin a little high or tucked near a doorway-like angle, then settle lower as Jenny approaches the shoebox, as if the space is softening around her. It should never feel like spying; it feels like the bedroom knows this child and is making room for her secret.
treatments.movementVersusStillness: Jenny’s movement is small against a large still room. The more she tries to finish the action, the stiller the environment becomes. After the lid closes, hold on stillness until it becomes active. The shoebox opening must be extremely restrained: no bounce, no flourish, just the lid easing up enough to let the call out.
treatments.depthAndEnvironment: Use bedroom depth to create gentle isolation. Jenny and the shoebox occupy a pocket of floor space, while the bed, wall, and shadows recede in soft layers. The darkness later should not feel scary; it should feel like everything is listening. The golden signal travels through this depth as a thin request, not a blast.
treatments.rhythmAndEscalation: The rhythm is breath-based: Jenny enters with held-in energy, speaks too lightly, folds and closes on a swallowed beat, then the room exhales into night. The call escalates by subtraction: fewer sounds, less movement, less visible detail, until the small hum and narrow light become the only things happening.
treatments.cutPhilosophy: Let wide frames endure past the obvious end of each action. Do not cut away the moment the lid shuts; the aftermath is the point. Use time passage sparingly and cleanly, preserving the sense that the same room has changed from ordinary bedroom to listening chamber.
treatments.openingImage: Jenny crossing into a wide, quiet bedroom space with the worksheet held close and the decorated shoebox waiting in a pool of ordinary evening dimness.
treatments.closingImage: A dark, breathing-wide view of Jenny asleep while, across the room, the shoebox gives off one narrow golden line, small enough to be secret and bright enough to be answered.
treatments.cinematographerChallenge: The conventional version would make the room merely background. Here the room must perform without becoming spooky or sentimental. The challenge is to shape negative space, soft shadow, and practical darkness so the audience feels pressure and care at once, while keeping the magic modest and emotionally precise.

treatmentSelection.selectedTreatment: The Shoebox Keeps the Secret, sharpened with the worksheet’s compression and the room’s held breath
combinedFrom: The Worksheet Gets Smaller, Then Louder
treatmentSelection.governingAudienceExperience: The audience feels quietly allowed into Jenny’s private attempt to make the hurt disappear, then feels the small warm lift that the thing she hid has been heard.
treatmentSelection.rationale: The strongest spine is The Shoebox Keeps the Secret because it keeps the scene emotionally human: Jenny’s trusted relationship with the shoebox is the story engine, not just the mechanics of paper or magic. It commits to wide, respectful observation, lets her hands and choices carry the shame, and understands that this scene must not fix Jenny yet. From The Worksheet Gets Smaller, we should take the physical clarity of compression: the worksheet becoming smaller through folding, then more present through tremble and light. That gives the feeling an observable screen life without needing explanation. From The Room Holds Its Breath, we should take the environmental hush after the lid closes: the bedroom becoming quieter, not scarier, so the golden seam feels like a tiny request pushing out of stillness. The combined approach gives us a clear emotional progression — denial, concealment, silence, signal — with strong visual rhyme between the lid closing and opening. It is feasible within the show’s wide-frame production model, memorable as a child-sized ritual, and specific to Jenny without overplaying her hurt.
treatmentSelection.rejectionChecks: No selected element depends on fixed character lanes, keeping every character visible, habitual action/reaction coverage, repeated close-up punctuation, mechanical shot counts, or generic decorative magic. The conventional version to reject would be standard bedside coverage: Jenny face close-up, worksheet insert, shoebox insert, reaction close-up, glow close-up. That would merely illustrate the script and over-prove the feeling. The Worksheet Gets Smaller, Then Louder is not selected alone because a pure object-story version risks turning the worksheet into the whole point and inviting insert-shot thinking; we keep its fold/tremble logic but reject any version where the paper replaces Jenny’s costly choice. The Room Holds Its Breath is not selected alone because an atmosphere-led version could become too abstract, with the bedroom performing the emotion instead of Jenny’s behaviour revealing it; we keep its negative space and hush but reject any version where the room becomes spooky, sentimental, or more important than the shoebox relationship. The selected treatment must stay wide, relational, and behaviour-led: Jenny, worksheet, shoebox, bed, floor space, lid, silence, then the narrow golden seam.

beats.sourceScript: In her bedroom, Jenny brings the folded worksheet to her decorated shoebox, a safe place for treasured things. She tries to make the feeling disappear by placing it inside and closing the lid, not noticing that the box has received more than paper: it has received the feeling she cannot carry alone.
exactDialogue: Jenny: It wasn’t even that funny.
Jenny: I don’t want to think about it.

orderedEvents.text: Shot 03: The Feeling Goes Into The Box
Jenny kneels on her bedroom floor.
Her decorated shoebox sits beside her bed. It has stars, hearts and one wonky rainbow drawn on the lid.
Inside are small treasures: a ribbon, a pebble, an old badge, a folded card.
She places the folded worksheet inside the box.
For a moment, she keeps her hand on it.

orderedEvents.speaker: Jenny
orderedEvents.text: I don’t want to think about it.
The box gives the smallest cardboard sigh.
Final Frame: The closed shoebox on the bedroom floor.

direction.premise: A classroom reading mistake follows Jenny home until her shoebox calls the Box Monsters into a handmade shame world built around one too-large wrong word.
direction.dramaticQuestion: Can the monsters help Jenny carry the mistake differently before shame makes her feel too small to try again?
direction.theme: Getting something wrong does not make you small.
direction.externalJourney: Jenny misreads a word, hides the worksheet in her shoebox, and the monsters travel from The Fold into a cardboard classroom where the mistaken word has swollen into the room’s bossy centrepiece. Their attempted fix fails, then they transform the machine and the meaning of the mistake so Jenny can face the word again.
direction.internalJourney: Jenny moves from public embarrassment, to hiding, to a tiny private openness, to reclaiming the mistake with humour, and finally to trying again while still feeling nervous.
direction.relationshipChanges: Patch begins as a brave responder who wants to help quickly, but earns Jenny’s echo’s trust by sitting with her instead of fixing her. Tilly shifts from controlling the outcome to redesigning her solution around emotional truth. Rumble protects space rather than forcing confidence. Nib’s odd humour becomes the safe bridge between shame and self-acceptance.
direction.emotionalCurve: Quiet pressure builds into embarrassment, then withdrawal, then magical concern. The middle tightens as the wrong fix makes shame heavier. Relief arrives first through being met gently, then through laughter that belongs to Jenny rather than at Jenny. The ending lands in soft courage and secret warmth.
direction.comedyCurve: The comedy starts as character imbalance in The Fold, turns into dry diagnosis and wonky tools, dips during the failed fix, then returns as Nib’s sideways cafe idea makes the mistake feel usable rather than poisonous. The final joke is small, affectionate and earned.
direction.setupPayoffMap: The word BRIDGE becomes BRIGGLE in class, then grows into the shame world’s looming word, then shrinks through laughter, becomes BRIDGE again, and returns in the classroom as a word Jenny can say. Jenny folds the worksheet smaller when ashamed, then later carries it without folding it. The Correct Answer Machine fails, then becomes the Try Again Machine. The shoebox’s first sigh and call pay off as its warm twitch and The Fold lamp glow.
direction.visualMotifs: Folding paper as shrinking self-worth; oversized lettering as shame taking up too much space; golden tape and cards as repair, not erasure; cardboard walls pressing inward and later opening with warmth; the shoebox as a private container that becomes a gentle doorway.
direction.sonicMotifs: Classroom quiet, tiny laugh, bell, cardboard sigh, pulse through floorboards, Fold honk, echoing repeated mistake, clunking machine, soft laugh, warm final glow.
direction.climax: Patch names the emotional truth that being wrong did not make Jenny small, allowing Tilly to change the machine’s purpose and Jenny’s echo to receive the golden repair card.
direction.resolution: Jenny wakes to the repaired worksheet and card, returns to class, reads the line correctly, gently jokes about the earlier mistake, and smiles as the secret magic remains unseen.
direction.intendedFinalFeeling: A warm, private courage: the feeling is still remembered, but it is no longer bigger than Jenny.

orderedEvents.text: Shot 03: The Feeling Goes Into The Box
Jenny kneels on her bedroom floor.
Her decorated shoebox sits beside her bed. It has stars, hearts and one wonky rainbow drawn on the lid.
Inside are small treasures: a ribbon, a pebble, an old badge, a folded card.
She places the folded worksheet inside the box.
For a moment, she keeps her hand on it.

showrunnerJudgement: PASS. The scene holds the selected experience: Jenny’s private attempt to make the worksheet disappear remains quiet, behavioural, and child-clear, and the later shoebox call feels like a small warm alert rather than a rescue. The storyboard avoids face-proof coverage and lets the paper, lid, floor space, and Jenny’s careful handling carry the shame. The emotional argument is visible in accumulated behaviour: she tries to minimise the hurt, folds the evidence smaller, trusts the shoebox with it, closes the lid, then sleeps while the box answers what she cannot yet face.
treatmentComparison: This remains close to the selected treatment. The camera position is correctly respectful and low, the shoebox is treated as an important piece of the room rather than a prop insert, and the first half is led by Jenny’s physical denial instead of explanatory emotion. The cut to the sleeping-room state is motivated by the treatment’s emotional transfer from Jenny’s point of view to the shoebox. The final image also preserves the contract: Jenny asleep beyond, lid open only a crack, a restrained golden seam, and the worksheet trembling as the hidden feeling becomes a call. The central experience has not been lost; it still feels like being allowed into a private after-school moment, then noticing that the trusted box has understood her.
packingJudgement: PACKING PASS. Two adjacent units total exactly 30 seconds, so the split needed a real protected boundary. It has one: the scripted “Later” with Jenny asleep is a time shift and a point-of-view transfer, not an avoidable editorial join. Keeping the whole scene as one continuous unit could blur the finality of Jenny closing the lid and make the box answer feel too immediate. The split protects the hush after concealment and the fresh anchor for the shoebox’s call. Stage counts are within standard and neither card is padded.
